newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Ebola is just a dumb macho virus, expert says.
newsitem.headline: Ebola is just a dumb macho virus, expert says.

text.p: The impact of Ebola, the dumb macho among killer viruses, is small compared with HIV but the media fanfare about it has boosted transatlantic cooperation on fighting epidemics, a leading expert said on Thursday.

"Ebola is a lot less smart than HIV (the virus that causes AIDS)," Guido van der Groen of the Antwerp Institute of Tropical Medicine told Reuters at the first day of a three-day colloquium on Ebola virus research.

But he said the terrifying virus, which inspired headlines because of the speed at which it strikes and causes internal organs to deteriorate, served as catalyst in the fight against other infectuous diseases.

"It's contributed to piling pressure on decision makers. It helped develop initiatives at the highest level between Europe and the United States to try and make an inventory of infectuous diseases and help coordinate surveillance," he said.
He said it had still not been possible to register all the people infected with HIV, which was isolated in 1983.
"It's an enormous task which requires an enormous amount of coordination...The emphasis is again being put on this by Ebola," he said.
Van der Groen, a renowned AIDS researcher, said the media attention for Ebola, named after a river in Zaire where it first struck, had been unique.

The virus, which causes massive internal bleeding and an excruciating death and has no known cure, was first identified at the Antwerp Institute in 1976 from blood samples of a Belgian nun working in northern Zaire.

But van der Groen said he dismantled his Ebola lab in 1984 and set up an AIDS lab with fellow Belgian doctor Peter Piot, now executive director of the United Nations' global AIDS agency, for examining the HIV virus.
"You have to make priorities and I needed every square centimetre to work on HIV," van der Groen said.

A total of about 1,000 people had so far been stricken by Ebola, with a death rate of between 70 and 80 percent. "But what is the effect on society? It's peanuts compared with other problems," he said.
"If they call Ebola a killer what would you say to a virus like HIV or hepatitis B. I call Ebola a macho because it immediately wants to prove it's there," he said.
Van der Groen played down any possibility that Ebola could ever reach such a wide scale as HIV, which has infected at least 40 million people.
HIV enters the body without sign and people remain infected for the rest of their lives. People carry the virus without being aware of it for 10 years...It's a sly virus," he said.

"For Ebola on the other hand people know within two or three days it entered their body and they can tell doctors, relatives he or she is ill. And if suddenly in a village 10 or 15 people have it they are isolated," he said.

But Van der Groen said Ebola outbreaks were not stopped by "so-called interventions of so-called Western medicine" and the virus would continue to strike for as long as the infrastructure in many developing countries remained poor.
